idiom_name: Ktor Authentication plugin + route-scoped authorization plugin (Ktor) / Spring Security method security
implementation_notes: In Ktor, authenticate("provider") { ... } is the identity gate, not by itself an authorization decision: routes nested in it run only for callers the provider validated, and call.principal<JWTPrincipal>() supplies the subject. Put the authorization decision in one route-scoped custom plugin using onCallValidators or the AuthenticationChecked hook, then respond with 403 and finish the call before the handler; the documented custom-plugin seam is the enforcement point for role, scope and resource checks. Ktor's type-safe authentication can also perform opt-in role checks, while Spring-based Kotlin uses @PreAuthorize and AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor. Keep role-to-permission mapping in one component and let routing only declare the guarded group.
pitfalls: Routes declared outside the authenticate block or without the route-scoped authorization plugin -> they are unprotected by construction -> group whole feature route sets and keep a fallback deny at the application boundary.

Using authenticate() as if it checked permissions -> an authenticated caller reaches an unauthorized handler -> enforce roles/scopes in the plugin's onCallValidators/AuthenticationChecked hook, not in each handler.

Reading call.principal() from a background coroutine after the request ends -> the request-bound subject is unavailable or wrong -> capture the verified subject and pass it explicitly to the job's own authorization boundary.
